docs.title: About
docs.text:
• This documentation is about an open source Python programming language package built for Odia language.
  • openodia is a Python package which contains various tools on Odia language.
  • The short term goal of this package is to not make state-of-the-art methods, but to make tools which work.
  • The documentation has been written to help you easily copy the code snippets and try out in your Python IDLE or iPython or Jupyter Notebook.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
• Set up the library from PyPI using the following command in your terminal or command prompt.
  • Requires Python 3.11 or higher.

  • The library is tested on Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15.

    Python Installation instruction

    You can download Python from Python official website and install on your system.

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text: pip install openodia

docs.title: Using uv (recommended)
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package installer and resolver.

# Install uv if you haven't already
pip install uv

# Install openodia
uv pip install openodia

# Or add to your project
uv add openodia

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
If you want to install from the source with latest changes:

git clone https://github.com/soumendrak/openodia.git
cd openodia
uv sync  # or: pip install -e .

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
The tools are available in Odia language.

  • Odia Alphabets
  • Generate random Odia names
  • Detect Odia Language
  • Word Tokenizer
  • Remove stopwords
  • Google Translate
  • Automatic extractive text summarization
  • Add Dictionary corpus
  • Unicode normalization & clean
  • Corpus statistics
  • Syllabifier (akshara)
  • Command-line interface
  • Translation cache configuration
  • Numbers, dates, and currency in words
  • Sentence segmenter
  • PII detection and masking

docs.title: Unicode normalization
docs.text:
• The same visible Odia string can be encoded in many byte sequences (e.g. precomposed vs decomposed nukta ଡ଼, stray ZWJ/ZWNJ from copy-paste, Latin digits mixed in with Odia).
  • Normalize text before tokenizing, indexing, hashing, or comparing.
from openodia import normalize, clean

# Pure Unicode normalization (NFC / NFD / NFKC / NFKD)
normalize("ଡ" + "଼")           # "ଡ଼"  (composed)
normalize("ଡ଼", form="NFD")    # "ଡ" + "଼"  (decomposed)

# Opinionated cleanup: NFC + strip ZWJ/ZWNJ + collapse whitespace
clean("  ନମ‌ସ୍କାର   ଓଡ଼ିଆ  ")
# "ନମସ୍କାର ଓଡ଼ିଆ"

# Optional digit conversion (off by default)
from openodia.text import CleanOptions
clean("ଆଜି 123 ବର୍ଷ", options=CleanOptions(latin_to_odia_digits=True))
# "ଆଜି ୧୨୩ ବର୍ଷ"

clean("ଆଜି ୧୨୩ ବର୍ଷ", options=CleanOptions(odia_to_latin_digits=True))
# "ଆଜି 123 ବର୍ଷ"
clean() is idempotent

clean(clean(x)) == clean(x) always holds, so it is safe to apply repeatedly or sprinkle through a pipeline without compounding side-effects.

docs.title: Corpus statistics
docs.text:
• N-grams, frequency distribution, collocations, and co-occurrence — pure-stdlib utilities for corpus exploration.
  • All functions accept either a pre-tokenised list[str] or a raw string (auto-tokenised via ud.word_tokenizer).
from openodia import FreqDist, ngrams, collocations, cooccurrence

tokens = "ରାମ ସୀତା ରାମ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ".split()

# N-grams (generator)
list(ngrams(tokens, 2))
# [('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'), ('ସୀତା', 'ରାମ'), ('ରାମ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ')]

# Frequency distribution — a Counter subclass with hapaxes / entropy / TTR.
fd = FreqDist(tokens)
fd.most_common(2)        # [('ରାମ', 2), ('ସୀତା', 1)]
fd.hapaxes()             # ['ସୀତା', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ']
fd.entropy()             # Shannon entropy (bits)
fd.ttr                   # type-token ratio

# PMI-scored bigram collocations.
collocations(tokens, top_k=5, min_count=1)
# [(('ରାମ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ'), 1.0), ...]

# Co-occurrence within a window (symmetric by default).
cooccurrence(tokens, window=2)
# Counter({('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'): 2, ...})
v1 scope
  • collocations ships PMI scoring only. Log-likelihood and chi-square are easy follow-ups.
  • Plot helpers are intentionally out of scope to keep the base install free of matplotlib.

docs.title: Syllabifier
docs.text:
• Splits a word into aksharas (orthographic syllables) using the Odia Unicode block rules: independent vowels, consonant clusters joined by halant (୍), matras, modifiers, and nukta.
  • Useful for TTS frontends, hyphenation/typography, character-level ML, and readability scoring.
from openodia import syllable

syllable.split("ନମସ୍କାର")        # ['ନ', 'ମ', 'ସ୍କା', 'ର']
syllable.split("ଓଡ଼ିଆ")            # ['ଓ', 'ଡ଼ି', 'ଆ']
syllable.split("ବିଦ୍ୟାଳୟ")        # ['ବି', 'ଦ୍ୟା', 'ଳ', 'ୟ']

syllable.count("ବିଦ୍ୟାଳୟ")        # 4

syllable.hyphenate("ବିଦ୍ୟାଳୟ")    # 'ବି-ଦ୍ୟା-ଳ-ୟ'
syllable.hyphenate("ନମସ୍କାର ଓଡ଼ିଆ", separator="·")
# 'ନ·ମ·ସ୍କା·ର ଓ·ଡ଼ି·ଆ'
Round-trip property

"".join(syllable.split(word)) == word for any input — the splitter is a strict tokeniser, never modifying or normalising characters.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
• Installing the package adds an openodia command. Each subcommand wraps a function from the library so they're scriptable from any shell.
  • Add --json to a subcommand for one machine-readable JSON document on stdout. This needs a release newer than 0.1.14: PyPI 0.1.14 has --json on detect-language only, and other subcommands exit with code 2 there. See AGENTS.md for the JSON shapes and exit codes, and llms.txt for an index aimed at AI agents.
  • Pass - as the text argument to read from stdin. Pass --file to read the text argument from a UTF-8 file; without it, an argument is always literal text, even if it matches a file name.
openodia --help

# Tokenisation
openodia tokenize "ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା ଆସୁଛନ୍ତି"
openodia tokenize --file input.txt --sentences

# Normalisation / cleanup
openodia normalize --file input.txt --form NFC
openodia clean "  ନମ‌ସ୍କାର  ଓଡ଼ିଆ  " --latin-to-odia

# Translation
openodia translate "ନମସ୍କାର!ଭଲ ଲାଗୁଛି?" --from or --to en
echo "hello! feeling good?" | openodia translate - --from en --to or

# Language detection
openodia detect-language "ନମସ୍କାର" --json

# Random Odia names
openodia name --kind first --count 5

# Extractive summary
openodia summarize --file article.txt --threshold 3

# Find or mask phone, email, Aadhaar, PAN, PIN code
openodia pii "ମୋ ଫୋନ ୯୮୭୬୫୪୩୨୧୦" --mask

# Stopword removal + corpus stats
openodia remove-stopwords "ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା"
openodia ngrams "ରାମ ସୀତା ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ" -n 2
openodia freq --file corpus.txt --top 20

docs.title: Translation cache
docs.text:
• Translations are memoised in an LRU. Defaults to 10,000 entries in memory.
  • Resize the cache, plug in a persistent disk backend, or inspect hit/miss counters.
  • Environment variables OPENODIA_CACHE_MAX_SIZE and OPENODIA_CACHE_DISK set defaults at process start.
from openodia import cache

cache.stats()
# {'hits': 0, 'misses': 0, 'size': 0, 'max_size': 10000, 'disk_size': 0}

# Resize the in-memory LRU.
cache.configure(max_size=50_000)

# Persist across runs (requires the [cache] extra: pip install openodia[cache]).
cache.configure(max_size=50_000, disk_path="~/.cache/openodia/translate")

cache.clear()
Disk persistence is opt-in

Disk persistence is gated behind the [cache] extra, which pulls in diskcache. Calling cache.configure(disk_path=...) without the extra raises a clear ImportError. The base install has no new dependency.

docs.title: Numbers and words
docs.text:
• Convert between integers and Odia words, in both Indian (lakh / crore) and short (million / billion / trillion) numbering scales.
  • Verbalise dates, currency amounts, and ordinals.
  • Bidirectional Odia ↔ ASCII digit conversion.
from openodia import numbers

# Cardinal numbers
numbers.to_words(1234)
# 'ଏକ ହଜାର ଦୁଇ ଶହ ଚଉତିରିଶ'

numbers.to_words(12_34_567)            # Indian: lakh / crore
# 'ବାର ଲକ୍ଷ ଚଉତିରିଶ ହଜାର ପାଞ୍ଚ ଶହ ସତଷଠି'

numbers.to_words(1_000_000, scale="short")
# 'ଏକ ମିଲିୟନ'

numbers.to_words(-100)
# 'ଋଣାତ୍ମକ ଏକ ଶହ'

# Reverse direction
numbers.from_words("ଏକ ହଜାର ଦୁଇ ଶହ ଚଉତିରିଶ")  # 1234

# Ordinals (1..10 irregular, 11+ uses 'ତମ' suffix)
numbers.to_ordinal(3)          # 'ତୃତୀୟ'
numbers.to_ordinal(11)         # 'ଏଗାରତମ'

# Currency
numbers.to_words_currency(1500.50)
# 'ଏକ ହଜାର ପାଞ୍ଚ ଶହ ଟଙ୍କା ପଚାଶ ପଇସା'

# Date verbalisation
from datetime import date
numbers.to_words_date(date(2026, 5, 27))
# '<day ordinal> ମଇ, ଦୁଇ ହଜାର ଛବିଶ'

# Digit conversion
numbers.ascii_to_odia("2026")   # '୨୦୨୬'
numbers.odia_to_ascii("୨୦୨୬")   # '2026'
Number words 0..99

The Odia counting table below 100 lives at openodia/numbers/_tables.py as a single tuple of length 100. Native-speaker corrections land there and are picked up by every API in this module automatically.

docs.title: Sentence segmenter
docs.text:
• Splits text into sentences on Odia (।, ॥) and Latin (., ?, !, …) terminators.
  • Decimal numbers (୨.୫, 2.5) and common abbreviations (ଡଃ, Dr., e.g.) do not trigger a split.
  • Each sentence keeps its terminator by default.
from openodia import sentences

sentences("ଆଜି ୨.୫ କୋଟି। ଆଗକୁ କଣ? ଭଲ ଦିନ!")
# ['ଆଜି ୨.୫ କୋଟି।', 'ଆଗକୁ କଣ?', 'ଭଲ ଦିନ!']

sentences("ଡଃ ସୁନୀତା ଆସିଲେ। ସେ କଲେଜରେ ପଢ଼ାନ୍ତି।")
# ['ଡଃ ସୁନୀତା ଆସିଲେ।', 'ସେ କଲେଜରେ ପଢ଼ାନ୍ତି।']

# Strict mode: only Odia terminators trigger splits.
sentences("Hi. ତୁମେ କେମିତି।", mode="strict")
# ['Hi. ତୁମେ କେମିତି।']

# Strip terminators
sentences("Hello. World!", keep_terminators=False)
# ['Hello', 'World']
Extending the abbreviations list

openodia.segment.ABBREVIATIONS is a public tuple. Project-specific vocabulary (e.g. trade names, place abbreviations) can be added by extending it in a wrapper module.

Existing ud.sentence_tokenizer is unchanged

The pre-existing helper continues to behave exactly as before (splits on " ।" only). Adopt openodia.sentences() for new code.

docs.title: PII detection and masking
docs.text:
• openodia.pii finds and masks personal identifiers in Odia text with patterns and one checksum. It is offline and adds no dependency. It needs a release newer than 0.1.14: openodia pii exits 2 on 0.1.14 and import openodia.pii fails there.
  • Odia digits (୦-୯) and ASCII digits are both recognised. Offsets in the result count characters of your original text. On the command line they count the text it read: --file drops a leading BOM and turns CRLF and a lone CR into LF. - (stdin) drops a leading BOM only and keeps any \r: a Linux or macOS pipe delivers \r\n unchanged, so offsets from - can differ from --file by one per line break.
  • Matches that overlap merge into one span typed by the longest match, so for every detected value no part of it stays visible; see the limits below. A tie goes to the earlier of EMAIL, URL, AADHAAR, PAN, PHONE, PINCODE. min_confidence is applied before merging.
  • openodia pii --json puts the raw matched text in every entity, so it contains the PII. Use --mask --json for output that holds only the masked text.
from openodia import pii

text = "ମୋ ଫୋନ ୯୮୭୬୫୪୩୨୧୦, ମେଲ a@b.com, ଆଧାର ୨୩୪୫ ୬୭୮୯ ୦୧୨୪, PIN ୭୫୧୦୦୧"
pii.detect(text)
# [PIIEntity(type='PHONE', text='୯୮୭୬୫୪୩୨୧୦', start=7, end=17, confidence=0.9), ...]
pii.mask(text)
# 'ମୋ ଫୋନ <PHONE>, ମେଲ <EMAIL>, ଆଧାର <AADHAAR>, PIN <PINCODE>'
pii.mask(text, types=["EMAIL"], placeholder=lambda entity: "***")
pii.detect(text, min_confidence=0.9)
Type What it matches Confidence PHONE 10-digit Indian mobile starting 6-9, optional +91, (+91), 0091, 91 followed by a space or -, or 0; optional space or - after the fifth digit 0.9 EMAIL local@domain.tld; the local part is up to 64 characters of letters, digits and . _ % + - ! # $ & ' * / = ? ^ ` { | } ~ (RFC 5322 atext), top-level domain of two or more letters. A longer local part is not found, and if it contains punctuation only its last 64 characters may be masked, so the earlier part stays visible; this is a deliberate limit left for a follow-up. A domain label over 63 characters is not matched: if it is the first label the whole address stays visible (a@ + 64 b + .com is unchanged), and a later one leaves a tail (a@x. + 64 b + .com gives <EMAIL>b.com). A local part that starts with non-ASCII letters, such as ଅଭିa@x.com, is masked only from the first ASCII character, so ଅଭି stays visible 0.95 URL http://, https:// or www. in any letter case, so HTTPS:// and WWW. are found (not glued to a letter, digit, @, . or - before it) up to whitespace; an apostrophe inside the URL is part of it (https://x.com/O'Connor?token=s is one <URL>), but one that closes a quoted URL is left out unless a URL character follows it ('https://a.com/x'+p, 'https://a.com/x'/y and 'https://a.com/x'9876543210 are masked to the end, which only over-masks), and so is one that ends the URL or comes before . , ; : ! ? ) ]; trailing . , ; : ! ? ) ] and । are left out 0.9 AADHAAR 12 digits starting 2-9, contiguous or grouped 4-4-4 by one space or -. 0.95 when the Verhoeff checksum passes, 0.5 when it fails 0.95 / 0.5 PAN AAAPA1234A: uppercase, fourth letter one of PCHFATBLJG 0.95 PINCODE 6 digits, first 1-9, directly after PIN, Pincode, PIN code or ପିନ 0.8

The wider local-part class can mask more than the address: leading delimiters can be swallowed, so key=val@host.com, ?q=a@b.com, path/to/a@c.com and price$5@x.com lose their prefix, `a@b.com`, 'a@b.com' and **a@b.com** swallow only the leading delimiter, ssh://git@host.com loses // (ssh://git@host has no top-level domain and stays unchanged), and www.x.com/a@b.com becomes <EMAIL> instead of <URL>; nothing leaks.

Confidence ranks how specific a pattern is; it is not a probability.

What it does not catch
  • Names, nicknames and addresses. A masked text can still identify a person, so this is not anonymisation.
  • Dates of birth, amounts, bank account and card numbers, landline numbers, passport and voter IDs.
  • Lowercase PAN, Aadhaar written with other separators or split by line breaks, and a PIN code with no PIN or ପିନ before it.
  • Aadhaar numbers starting with 0 or 1, which UIDAI does not issue.
  • A bare domain with no http(s):// or www., an email whose local part is over 64 characters (see the EMAIL row), and digits of other scripts such as Devanagari.
  • False positives: a 10-digit number starting 6-9 (an order or account number) is reported as PHONE even if nobody owns it, a 12-digit number starting 2-9 as AADHAAR at confidence 0.5, and a PAN-shaped code as PAN. Filter with types and min_confidence.
  • A bare 91 before a mobile number is taken as its country code only when a space or - follows it.
  • mask repeats detection and replacement until nothing changes, at most 10 passes, because masking a value can expose one that was glued to it, such as a PAN written right before a URL. With the default <TYPE> tags, masking its own output therefore changes nothing, unless the input chains more than 10 glued values. Past that, the text mask returns can still contain raw PII, so do not rely on it for input like that. A custom placeholder receives entities from the later passes too, with offsets into the partly masked text, and one that returns PII-shaped text, for example one that keeps the last four digits, can keep the loop running to its limit.
  • detect and mask raise TypeError for a text that is not a str or types given as a bare string, and ValueError for an unknown type or a min_confidence outside 0 to 1.
  • There is no pseudonymisation or reversible mapping: masking is one-way.

docs.title: Odia names
docs.text:
• You can generate Odia names using the name module with the following syntax:

from openodia import name
name.generate_names()
'''
['ଯଦୁମଣୀ ମାଢ଼ୀ', 'ବାସନ୍ତି ବ୍ରହ୍ମା', 'ପ୍ରବୀଣ ସିଂହ ମୁକ୍କିମ', 'ବୃନ୍ଦାବନ ଧଳ', 'ଅଶ୍ୱିନୀ କିଶୋର ଜଗଦେବ', 
 'ଶ୍ରୀଯୁକ୍ତ ଇରାଶିଷ ସେଠୀ', 'କୁମାରୀ ସୁମନ ସିଂଦେଓ', 'ସଲିଲ ଅଲ୍ଲୀ ଛତ୍ରିଆ', 'ଦିବାକରନାଥ ରାଧାରାଣୀ ଆଚାର୍ଯ୍ୟ', 'ଦୁର୍ଗା ସୁନ୍ଦରସୁର୍ଯ୍ୟା ପୁଟୀ']
'''
- By default, it will return ten randomly generated names. - If you want, you can generate more names by providing the number of names needed in the first argument.

from openodia import name
name.generate_names(20)
'''
['ସାବିତ୍ରୀ ଧଳ', 'ଶ୍ରୀଯୁକ୍ତ ଉତ୍କଳ ପାଳ', 'ଯଦୁମଣି ସୁବାହୁ', 'ପ୍ରେମଲତା ପମ', 'ଗୁରୁ ପୃଷ୍ଟି', 
 'ଗୀତା ଦାସବର୍ମା', 'କୁମାରୀ ଦୁର୍ଗା ବ୍ରହ୍ମା', 'କୁମାରୀ ପୁପୁଲ ହେମ୍ବ୍ରମ', 'ମକର ସାଇ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମୀକାନ୍ତ ନନ୍ଦି', 
 'ଶ୍ରୀ ଦୀନବନ୍ଧୁ ଲୋକ', 'କୁମାରୀ ଜିନା ଗଜପତି', 'ମୃଣାଳ ଭୂଷଣ ଛତ୍ରିଆ', 'ସୁଧାଂଶୁମାଳିନୀ ସିଂହ ସାଲୁଜା', 'ସୁଧାଂଶୁମାଳିନୀ ମହାନନ୍ଦ', 
 'ସୁମନୀ ନାଥ', 'କୁମାରୀ ନୀତୁ ହିକ୍କା', 'ଶ୍ରୀମତୀ ଲୀଳା କାଡାମ୍', 'ସନାତନ କୁଅଁର', 'କୁମାରୀ କବି ଦାସନାୟକ']
'''
- In addition to this, you can create specific name parts like prefix, first name, middle name, surname, etc. - By default you will get ten names. However, to get more number of results you can specify the number of names in the first argument.

from openodia import name
name.generate_firstnames()
'''
['ଅନିରୁଦ୍ଧ', 'ଦେବରାଜ', 'ଆଶ୍ରିତ', 'ବଦ୍ରି', 'ସଦାଶିବ', 
 'ପ୍ରଦିପ୍ତ', 'ଧୃବ', 'ଶ୍ରୀନାଥ', 'ସ୍ନିତି', 'ପ୍ରକୃତି']
'''

name.generate_prefixes()
'''
['ଶ୍ରୀଯୁକ୍ତ', 'ଶ୍ରୀମତୀ', 'କୁମାରୀ', 'ଶ୍ରୀମାନ', 'ସୁଶ୍ରୀ', 'ଶ୍ରୀ']
'''

name.generate_middlenames()
'''
['ଲେଖା', 'ଶ୍ରୀ', 'ମାଧବ', 'କେତନ', 'ଯୋଶେଫ୍', 
 'କେଶରୀ', 'ଭୂଷଣ', 'ରାଧାରାଣୀ', 'ମାନସିଂହ', 'କିଶୋର']
'''

name.generate_surnames()
'''
['ପରିଜା', 'ରଣସିଂହ', 'ମହାପାତ୍ର', 'ରଥ', 'ମହନ୍ତ', 
 'ବେହେରା', 'ଦେଓ', 'ଧଳ', 'ଦିଆନ', 'ହିମିରିକା']
'''

docs.title: Detect Odia Language
docs.text:
• A binary language classification method used which will return if the input text is in Odia language or in any other non-Odia language.
  • Along with this a confidence score also returned. The score provides how confident the library is that it is Odia or Non-Odia.
  • There is a threshold parameter to the method which can be configured to tune the confidence score threshold after which it will be regarded as Odia. The default value is 0.5.

from openodia import ud
ud.detect_language("hey how are you?")
'''
{'language': 'non-odia', 'confidence_score': 1.0}
'''

docs.title: Remove stopwords
docs.text:
• Frequently occurring words in a language are called as stopwords. Using the below function you can remove the stopwords.
  • Internally this method calls the word_tokenize method to get tokens from the text.
  • As most of the time processing happens in list by default a list of strings will be returned.

from openodia import ud
ud.remove_stopwords("ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା ଆମକୁ ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ ଦେଇଛନ୍ତି")
'''
['ରାମ', 'ସୀତା', 'ଆମକୁ', 'ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ']
'''

ud.remove_stopwords("ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା ଆମକୁ ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ ଦେଇଛନ୍ତି ", get_str=True)
'''
'ରାମ ସୀତା ଆମକୁ ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ'
'''
Here the stopwords ଓ and ଦେଇଛନ୍ତି are removed from the text.

docs.title: Customising the stopword list
docs.text:
STOPWORDS is a frozenset you can extend or replace per call. For richer workflows use the Stopwords class, which supports add / remove, loading from a file, deriving from a corpus, and saving back to disk.

from openodia import Stopwords, ud

# Start from the bundled list and tweak it.
sw = Stopwords.default().add("ପ୍ରାୟ").remove("ଓ")
ud.remove_stopwords("ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା", stopwords=sw)
# ['ରାମ', 'ଓ', 'ସୀତା']  — 'ଓ' kept because we removed it from the list

# Load a domain-specific list from disk.
legal = Stopwords.from_file("legal_stopwords.txt")
ud.remove_stopwords(article, stopwords=legal)

# Derive a list from corpus frequency.
auto = Stopwords.from_corpus(tokens, top_n=100)
auto.save("derived_stopwords.txt")

Any container supporting token in stopwords works — Stopwords, frozenset[str], set[str], or list[str]. The bundled STOPWORDS constant remains the default when the kwarg is omitted, so existing code keeps working unchanged.

docs.title: Translation
docs.text:
• The translation module is a wrapper on top of Google Translate API.
  • There are two translation methods provided:
    1. odia_to_other_lang and
    2. other_lang_to_odia

docs.title: other_lang_to_odia
docs.text:
• As the name suggests this function can be used to translate from any other language to Odia language.
  • If you are translating from any other language other than English, please provide the language code of it.
from openodia import other_lang_to_odia
other_lang_to_odia("hello! feeling good?")

'ନମସ୍କାର!ଭଲ ଲାଗୁଛି?'

docs.title: odia_to_other_lang
docs.text:
• This function can be used to translate an Odia text into another language.

docs.title: Offline Dictionary
docs.text:
• An offline dictionary will be downloaded as soon as you install this library.
  • Therefore, when you translate from English to Odia words/phrases it will hit the offline dictionary first, if not found it will go for the Google translate API.
  • Google Translate API responses have been cached, therefore from the 2nd call onwards on the same term(s) it will fetch fast from the local in-memory cache.
  • We have used LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with a maximum size of 10000.
English to Odia translation Workflow

Therefore, we have three flows on English to Odia dictionary translation:

  1. English text → Check in Offline dictionary → Found → Return result
  2. English text → Check in Offline dictionary → Not Found → Check in Cache → Found → Return result from Cache
  3. English text → Check in Offline dictionary → Not Found → Check in Cache → Not Found → Hit Google Translate API → Update the Cache → Return result

from openodia import name
name.generate_names()

['ଯଦୁମଣୀ ମାଢ଼ୀ', 'ବାସନ୍ତି ବ୍ରହ୍ମା', 'ପ୍ରବୀଣ ସିଂହ ମୁକ୍କିମ', 'ବୃନ୍ଦାବନ ଧଳ', 'ଅଶ୍ୱିନୀ କିଶୋର ଜଗଦେବ', 
 'ଶ୍ରୀଯୁକ୍ତ ଇରାଶିଷ ସେଠୀ', 'କୁମାରୀ ସୁମନ ସିଂଦେଓ', 'ସଲିଲ ଅଲ୍ଲୀ ଛତ୍ରିଆ', 'ଦିବାକରନାଥ ରାଧାରାଣୀ ଆଚାର୍ଯ୍ୟ', 'ଦୁର୍ଗା ସୁନ୍ଦରସୁର୍ଯ୍ୟା ପୁଟୀ']

Name morphology
  • In Odia names, mostly the surname carries the family name.
  • Therefore, there is a limited number of surnames, which can be used to identify names in a text.
Exceptions
  • There has been a trend recently where, after marriage the spouse add their in-law's surname; which makes two surnames in a single name.
  • However, recently there has been no surnames in the names or surname without any family name has been kept. Which needs to be kept an eye for.

docs.title: Data Masking
docs.text:
• As these names database has been taken from Wikipedia and actual person names in Odisha, you can use these as NER for person name recognition.
  • In data engineering projects when you need to ingest large amount of data, you need to mask or anonymize the PI (Personal Identification) data from the data source.
  • This is to remove bias and increase privacy on your data/model.

docs.title: Masking phone numbers, emails, Aadhaar, PAN and PIN codes
docs.text: • openodia.pii.mask(text) replaces them with <PHONE>, <EMAIL>, <AADHAAR>, <PAN>, <PINCODE> and <URL> tags. See PII detection and masking for what it does and does not catch. It does not mask names. openodia pii exits 2 on 0.1.14 and import openodia.pii fails there; it needs a newer release.

docs.title: Masking names:
docs.text:
• To avoid disrupting privacy of individuals, you can identify the names of people in the text and
  • Replace the names with a mask tag like <name>.
  • Example
    • ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି । has potential personal data that which a person can derive like:
      1. ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ is married.
      2. ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ is male.
      3. He has a car.
      4. He is in Puri.
    • To avoid this kind of personal privacy exposure, we need to mask the text to <name> ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି ।
  • The problem with this method is you miss the credibility of an important feature of the input data. As there is no uniqueness among the name field.

docs.title: Anonymization of names:
docs.text:
• Using this method rather than completely removing all names with a <name> tag you can substitute with a fake name.
  • It maintains the uniqueness of the name field.
  • However, in many cases you may need to revert back to the original person name after a certain operation has been completed. That's not possible as anonymization is an irreversible procedure.
  • Example
    • ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି । will be anonymized as ବ୍ରଜମୋହନ ପଣ୍ଡା ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି ।
    • Did you notice how ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ has changed to ବ୍ରଜମୋହନ ପଣ୍ଡା?
  • Here are some situations in which you may want to use anonymization:1
    • If you no longer need to communicate or work with a consumer, but wish to archive their activity, order history, or any other details that could not be used to identify them.
    • To perform data analyses that are unrelated to the services you provide the consumer.
    • If you need to make data available to a group of people outside those that are designated to fulfill your services, such as a wide group of employees or consultants.

docs.title: Pseudonimization of names:
docs.text:
• This is same as anonymization, with only difference that, the anonymized names can be replaced with their original names.
  • Example
    • ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି । will be pseudonymized as hrtvd6wqbvs4320 ବାବୁ ସସ୍ତ୍ରୀକ ନିଜ କାରରେ ବସି ପୁରୀ ବୁଲିଯାଇଛନ୍ତି ।
    • Did you notice how ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ has changed to hrtvd6wqbvs4320?
    • Here hrtvd6wqbvs4320 has shown as a demonstration of a key, which can be stored in a hash table with value as ବୈଦ୍ୟନାଥ ସିଂହଦେଓ.
    • This text can be further reversed by referring to this hash table or a unique private key.
  • Data pseudonymization can be used when you will need to re-identify users in the future:1
    • To keep data secure during the fulfillment of services, by masking identifying details to employees or other data handlers that do not need those details.
    • To maintain data protection within your database or records, order histories, and inactive customers that you remain in contact with.
    • To transfer data over international borders.
    • To maintain data protection and Privacy by Design principles laid out by the GDPR.

docs.title: cache
docs.text:
Translation cache configuration and observability.

The package keeps an in-memory LRU of translation results. By default it holds 10,000 entries and is hidden from callers.

Use the helpers in this module to:

  • enlarge / shrink the LRU,
  • enable a persistent disk cache (requires the [cache] extra),
  • observe hit/miss counts,
  • clear the cache.

Configuration may also be set via environment variables at import time:

  • OPENODIA_CACHE_MAX_SIZE — integer LRU size (default 10000).
  • OPENODIA_CACHE_DISK — path to a directory used for disk persistence.
Example

from openodia import cache cache.configure(max_size=50_000) cache.stats()

docs.title: Corpus statistics and summarization
docs.text: Count and rank words, find word pairs that belong together, and pull the key sentences out of a text. Every example on this page is run by the test suite.

docs.title: N-grams
docs.text:
ngrams yields tuples of n consecutive tokens, lazily. It takes a list of tokens or a raw string, which is tokenized with ud.word_tokenizer.

>>> from openodia import ngrams
>>> tokens = "ରାମ ସୀତା ରାମ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ".split()
>>> list(ngrams(tokens, 2))
[('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'), ('ସୀତା', 'ରାମ'), ('ରାମ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ')]
>>> list(ngrams("ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ", 2))
[('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'), ('ସୀତା', 'ଘରକୁ')]
>>> list(ngrams(tokens, 5))
[]
>>> list(ngrams(tokens, 0))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: n must be >= 1, got 0

Gotcha: errors appear when you iterate

ngrams is a generator, so the ValueError for n < 1 is raised on the first next(), not when you call it. Wrap it in list() or loop over it to see the error.

docs.title: Frequency distribution
docs.text:
FreqDist is a collections.Counter with a few extras. An empty distribution reports 0.0 for ttr and entropy() instead of dividing by zero.

>>> from openodia import FreqDist
>>> fd = FreqDist(tokens)
>>> fd.most_common(2)
[('ରାମ', 2), ('ସୀତା', 1)]
>>> fd.hapaxes()
['ସୀତା', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ']
>>> fd.total_count, fd.ttr
(4, 0.75)
>>> fd.entropy()
1.5
>>> FreqDist().ttr
0.0

hapaxes() are the tokens seen once, ttr is the type-token ratio (distinct tokens divided by all tokens) and entropy() is the Shannon entropy in bits.

docs.title: Collocations
docs.text:
collocations ranks bigrams by pointwise mutual information (PMI). Bigrams seen fewer than min_count times are skipped, and the default is 2.

>>> from openodia import collocations
>>> [(pair, round(score, 3)) for pair, score in collocations(tokens, top_k=2, min_count=1)]
[(('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'), 1.415), (('ସୀତା', 'ରାମ'), 1.415)]
>>> collocations(tokens)
[]

Gotcha: a short text yields no results

The second call returns [] because no bigram in the four-token sample occurs twice. Lower min_count for small inputs. PMI also favors rare pairs, so keep min_count at 2 or more on real corpora.

docs.title: Co-occurrence
docs.text:
cooccurrence counts how often two tokens appear within window positions of each other. By default pairs are sorted so (a, b) and (b, a) count together. Pass symmetric=False to keep the order.

>>> from openodia import cooccurrence
>>> cooccurrence(tokens, window=1)
Counter({('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'): 2, ('ରାମ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ'): 1})
>>> cooccurrence(tokens, window=1, symmetric=False)
Counter({('ରାମ', 'ସୀତା'): 1, ('ସୀତା', 'ରାମ'): 1, ('ରାମ', 'ଲକ୍ଷ୍ମଣ'): 1})

docs.title: Summarization
docs.text:
WordFrequency is an extractive summarizer. After stopwords are removed it keeps the words that occur more than threshold times, then returns every sentence that contains one of them. When you leave threshold out, it is the number of tokens divided by the number of distinct tokens.

>>> from openodia import WordFrequency
>>> text = "ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ । ସେ ଭଲ ଲୋକ । ରାମ ଭଲ ପିଲା । ଓଡ଼ିଶା ଏକ ସୁନ୍ଦର ରାଜ୍ୟ । ପୁରୀରେ ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ ମନ୍ଦିର ଅଛି । ରାମ ପୁରୀକୁ ଯାଏ ।"
>>> wf = WordFrequency(text)
>>> wf.get_summary()
'ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ  ସେ ଭଲ ଲୋକ  ରାମ ଭଲ ପିଲା  ରାମ ପୁରୀକୁ ଯାଏ'
>>> wf.get_summary(threshold=2)
'ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ  ରାମ ଭଲ ପିଲା  ରାମ ପୁରୀକୁ ଯାଏ'
>>> wf.get_summary(threshold=3)
''

A higher threshold gives a shorter summary, and a threshold above every word count gives an empty string.

Gotchas

  • The summary drops the । terminators and joins the kept sentences with two spaces.
  • A word matches a sentence by substring, so ରାମ also selects a sentence that only contains a longer word starting with ରାମ.
  • threshold=0 means "not given" and falls back to the automatic value.
  • Sentences are split with ud.sentence_tokenizer, so the text must use । (a space, then the full stop) between sentences.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Installing the package adds an openodia command. Each subcommand wraps one library function, reads its text from an argument, a file or stdin, and prints plain text or JSON. Every example on this page is run by the test suite.

Exit codes, error messages and the JSON shape of every subcommand are specified in AGENTS.md. This page covers how to use the commands.

docs.title: Where the text comes from
docs.text:
The text argument is literal text. Pass - to read stdin, or add --file to treat the argument as the path of a UTF-8 file.

$ openodia tokenize "ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ । ସେ ଭଲ"
ରାମ
ସୀତା
ଘରକୁ
ଯାଏ
।
ସେ
ଭଲ
$ echo "ରାମ ଓ ସୀତା" | openodia remove-stopwords -
ରାମ
ସୀତା
$ printf "ରାମ ସୀତା" > input.txt
$ openodia tokenize input.txt
input
txt
$ openodia tokenize input.txt --file
ରାମ
ସୀତା

Gotcha: a file name without --file is just text

openodia tokenize input.txt tokenizes the string input.txt, as the third command above shows, even when that file exists.

docs.title: Text and JSON output
docs.text:
The default output is meant for reading and for grep, sort and wc. Add --json for one JSON document on stdout.

Needs a release newer than 0.1.14

--json on every subcommand is on main but not in PyPI 0.1.14. PyPI 0.1.14 has --json on detect-language only, and other subcommands exit with code 2 there. From a source checkout, uv run openodia <subcommand> --json works. See AGENTS.md for the JSON shapes and exit codes.

$ openodia tokenize "ରାମ ସୀତା" --json
{"tokens": ["ରାମ", "ସୀତା"]}
$ openodia detect-language "ନମସ୍କାର"
odia (confidence: 1.0)
$ openodia detect-language "ନମସ୍କାର" --json
{"language": "odia", "confidence_score": 1.0}

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A usage error such as a missing argument, or two options that exclude each other, exits with code 2 and prints the usage text. A runtime error such as a missing file prints openodia: error: ... and exits with code 1.

$ openodia clean "x" --latin-to-odia --odia-to-latin 2>&1 | tail -n 1
openodia clean: error: argument --odia-to-latin: not allowed with argument --latin-to-odia
$ openodia tokenize missing.txt --file 2>&1 || echo "exit code $?"
openodia: error: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'
exit code 1

docs.title: Numbers, dates and currency
docs.text: Convert integers to Odia words and back, verbalize dates and rupee amounts, and switch between Odia and ASCII digits. Every example on this page is run by the test suite.

docs.title: Cardinals
docs.text:
to_words takes an int. The default scale="indian" uses ଲକ୍ଷ (lakh) and କୋଟି (crore); scale="short" uses ମିଲିୟନ (million) and larger units.

>>> from openodia import numbers
>>> numbers.to_words(0)
'ଶୂନ୍ୟ'
>>> numbers.to_words(101)
'ଏକ ଶହ ଏକ'
>>> numbers.to_words(1234567)
'ବାର ଲକ୍ଷ ଚଉତିରିଶ ହଜାର ପାଞ୍ଚ ଶହ ସତଷଠି'
>>> numbers.to_words(12345678)
'ଏକ କୋଟି ତେଇଶ ଲକ୍ଷ ପଞ୍ଚଚାଳିଶ ହଜାର ଛଅ ଶହ ଅଠସତୁରୀ'
>>> numbers.to_words(1234567, scale="short")
'ଏକ ମିଲିୟନ ଦୁଇ ଶହ ଚଉତିରିଶ ହଜାର ପାଞ୍ଚ ଶହ ସତଷଠି'
>>> numbers.to_words(-100)
'ଋଣାତ୍ମକ ଏକ ଶହ'

from_words reverses it. It must be given the same scale that produced the words:

>>> numbers.from_words("ଏକ ହଜାର ଦୁଇ ଶହ")
1200
>>> numbers.from_words(numbers.to_words(987654321))
987654321
>>> numbers.from_words("ଏକ ମିଲିୟନ", scale="short")
1000000
>>> numbers.from_words("ଏକ ମିଲିୟନ")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: unrecognised token: 'ମିଲିୟନ'

Gotcha: errors for bad input

from_words raises ValueError for a word it does not know, which includes short-scale words read with the default Indian scale (as above). to_words(1.5) raises TypeError, but only as a side effect of the integer-only implementation, not as a deliberate check, so do not rely on the exception type or message. bool is an int in Python, so to_words(True) returns ଏକ.

docs.title: Ordinals
docs.text:
Ordinals from 1 to 10 are irregular. From 11 on, the suffix ତମ is added to the cardinal.

>>> numbers.to_ordinal(1), numbers.to_ordinal(2), numbers.to_ordinal(10)
('ପ୍ରଥମ', 'ଦ୍ୱିତୀୟ', 'ଦଶମ')
>>> numbers.to_ordinal(11), numbers.to_ordinal(21)
('ଏଗାରତମ', 'ଏକୋଇଶତମ')
>>> numbers.to_ordinal(0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: ordinals are defined for n >= 1, got 0

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
to_words_date accepts a date or datetime (the time part is ignored). The day is an ordinal and the year is spelled out.

>>> from datetime import date, datetime
>>> numbers.to_words_date(date(2000, 1, 1))
'ପ୍ରଥମ ଜାନୁଆରୀ, ଦୁଇ ହଜାର'
>>> numbers.to_words_date(datetime(2026, 10, 27, 5, 30))
'ସତାଇଶତମ ଅକ୍ଟୋବର, ଦୁଇ ହଜାର ଛବିଶ'

docs.title: Currency
docs.text:
Only rupees ("INR") are supported. The fractional part is rounded half-up to two places and spoken as ପଇସା (paisa). A zero part is left out.

>>> numbers.to_words_currency(1500.50)
'ଏକ ହଜାର ପାଞ୍ଚ ଶହ ଟଙ୍କା ପଚାଶ ପଇସା'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(1)
'ଏକ ଟଙ୍କା'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(0.05)
'ପାଞ୍ଚ ପଇସା'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(0)
'ଶୂନ୍ୟ ଟଙ୍କା'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(1234.5, scale="short")
'ଏକ ହଜାର ଦୁଇ ଶହ ଚଉତିରିଶ ଟଙ୍କା ପଚାଶ ପଇସା'
>>> from decimal import Decimal
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(Decimal("10.25"))
'ଦଶ ଟଙ୍କା ପଚିଶ ପଇସା'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(5, currency="USD")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: unsupported currency 'USD'; supported: 'INR'
>>> numbers.to_words_currency(-5)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: amount must be >= 0, got -5

Gotcha: prefer Decimal for money

A float is converted with Decimal(str(amount)), so 1500.50 is exact. Values you computed with float arithmetic can still carry rounding error before they get here.

docs.title: Digits
docs.text:
ascii_to_odia and odia_to_ascii convert digits inside a longer string and leave every other character as it is.

>>> numbers.ascii_to_odia("Call 100 ଆଜି 2026")
'Call ୧୦୦ ଆଜି ୨୦୨୬'
>>> numbers.odia_to_ascii("୧୨୩ abc")
'123 abc'

docs.title: Script, syllables and names
docs.text: The Odia character inventory, a syllable splitter, and a generator of Odia names. Every example on this page is run by the test suite.

docs.title: Alphabet
docs.text:
alphabet exposes the Odia Unicode block as plain list objects of single characters: all_letters, vowels, consonants, matras (vowel signs and other combining marks), numbers and punctuations.

>>> from openodia import alphabet
>>> alphabet.vowels
['ଅ', 'ଆ', 'ଇ', 'ଈ', 'ଉ', 'ଊ', 'ଋ', 'ଌ', 'ଏ', 'ଐ', 'ଓ', 'ଔ']
>>> len(alphabet.consonants), len(alphabet.numbers)
(34, 10)
>>> "କ" in alphabet.consonants, "କ" in alphabet.vowels
(True, False)
>>> alphabet.matras[:6]
['ଁ', 'ଂ', 'ଃ', '଼', 'ଽ', 'ା']

Gotcha: matras includes more than vowel signs

The list also holds the candrabindu, anusvara, visarga, nukta, avagraha and virama, plus the ai length mark ୖ, the au length mark ୗ, the isshar ୰, the letter wa ୱ and the fraction sign ୲. It is the set of combining marks and signs, not only the matras of the textbook chart.

Gotcha: the lists are shared

Each attribute is one list object for the whole process. Copy it with list(alphabet.vowels) before you sort or mutate it.

A common use is counting how much of a string is Odia script:

>>> odia = set(alphabet.all_letters)
>>> sum(ch in odia for ch in "ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଭାଷା abc")
9

docs.title: Syllables
docs.text:
syllable.split breaks a word into orthographic syllables: a consonant with its vowel sign, or a conjunct (consonant + virama + consonant) with its vowel sign. count returns how many there are and hyphenate joins them with a separator.

>>> from openodia import syllable
>>> syllable.split("ନମସ୍କାର")
['ନ', 'ମ', 'ସ୍କା', 'ର']
>>> syllable.split("ପ୍ରଥମ")
['ପ୍ର', 'ଥ', 'ମ']
>>> syllable.count("ବିଦ୍ୟାଳୟ")
4
>>> syllable.hyphenate("ବିଦ୍ୟାଳୟ")
'ବି-ଦ୍ୟା-ଳ-ୟ'
>>> syllable.hyphenate("ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଭାଷା", separator="·")
'ଓ·ଡ଼ି·ଆ ଭା·ଷା'
>>> syllable.split("")
[]

Gotcha: the split is orthographic

split follows the written script, so it does not model schwa deletion or pronunciation. Characters that are not Odia are returned one by one, and spaces are returned as their own item.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
name produces random Odia names. Part generators sample without replacement, and asking for more than the list holds returns the whole list.

>>> from openodia import name
>>> len(name.generate_firstnames(count=3))
3
>>> len(name.generate_surnames(count=4))
4
>>> len(name.generate_prefixes(count=2)), len(name.generate_middlenames(count=2))
(2, 2)
>>> set(name.generate_firstnames(count=3, name_type="male")) <= set(name.generate_firstnames(count=10**6, name_type="male"))
True
>>> len(name.generate_names(count=5))
5

name_type accepts "male", "female" or "unisex" (case-insensitive). An empty value mixes all first names. Anything else raises ValueError:

>>> name.generate_firstnames(name_type="robot")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Invalid name_type provided

Gotcha: two sources, two behaviours

The part generators (generate_firstnames, generate_surnames, ...) sample from lists shipped in the package with random.sample. generate_names instead calls the or_IN locale of Faker once per name and does not de-duplicate.

For use cases such as masking and anonymizing names in a text, see Applications.

docs.title: Text processing
docs.text: Tokenize, split into sentences, remove stopwords, normalize and detect the language of Odia text. Every example on this page is run by the test suite, so the output shown is what the current release prints.

docs.title: Tokenize words
docs.text:
ud.word_tokenizer splits on whitespace and ASCII punctuation. The Odia full stop । is kept as its own token because it is not in the separator set.

>>> from openodia import ud
>>> text = "ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ । ସେ ଭଲ ଲୋକ ।"
>>> ud.word_tokenizer(text)
['ରାମ', 'ସୀତା', 'ଘରକୁ', 'ଯାଏ', '।', 'ସେ', 'ଭଲ', 'ଲୋକ', '।']
>>> ud.word_tokenizer("")
[]

Gotcha: the hyphen is a separator

ud.word_tokenizer("ଉପ-ପାରମାଣବିକ") returns two tokens. If you need hyphenated words kept whole, split on whitespace yourself with str.split().

docs.title: Split into sentences
docs.text:
Two helpers exist and they behave differently.

sentences is the one to use for new code. It understands Odia (।, ॥) and Latin (., ?, !) terminators and does not split on decimals or abbreviations.

>>> from openodia import sentences
>>> sentences(text)
['ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ।', 'ସେ ଭଲ ଲୋକ।']
>>> sentences("ଆଜି ୨.୫ କୋଟି ଟଙ୍କା। ଆଗକୁ କଣ?")
['ଆଜି ୨.୫ କୋଟି ଟଙ୍କା।', 'ଆଗକୁ କଣ?']
>>> sentences("ଡଃ ସୁନୀତା ଆସିଲେ। ସେ କଲେଜରେ ପଢ଼ାନ୍ତି।")
['ଡଃ ସୁନୀତା ଆସିଲେ।', 'ସେ କଲେଜରେ ପଢ଼ାନ୍ତି।']
>>> sentences("Hi. ତୁମେ କେମିତି।", mode="strict")
['Hi. ତୁମେ କେମିତି।']
>>> sentences("Hello. World!", keep_terminators=False)
['Hello', 'World']

ud.sentence_tokenizer only splits on the exact string " ।" (a space followed by the full stop). It keeps leading spaces and returns an empty last element when the text ends with ।.

>>> ud.sentence_tokenizer(text)
['ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ', ' ସେ ଭଲ ଲୋକ', '']

Gotcha: sentences removes the space before ।

sentences(text) returns 'ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ।' for input 'ରାମ ସୀତା ଘରକୁ ଯାଏ ।'. The terminator is attached to the sentence and the space before it is dropped.

docs.title: Remove stopwords
docs.text:
ud.remove_stopwords accepts raw text or a list of tokens. It returns a list of tokens, or one string when get_str=True. The default list is openodia.STOPWORDS, a frozenset.

>>> ud.remove_stopwords("ଏହା ଏକ ସୁନ୍ଦର ଘର")
['ଏକ', 'ସୁନ୍ଦର', 'ଘର']
>>> ud.remove_stopwords(["ଏହା", "ଏକ", "ସୁନ୍ଦର", "ଘର"], get_str=True)
'ଏକ ସୁନ୍ଦର ଘର'
>>> from openodia import STOPWORDS
>>> type(STOPWORDS).__name__, len(STOPWORDS)
('frozenset', 63)

Passing a str tokenizes it first. The default list includes the full stop ।, so the । tokens are dropped as well:

>>> ud.remove_stopwords(text)
['ରାମ', 'ସୀତା', 'ଘରକୁ', 'ଯାଏ', 'ସେ', 'ଭଲ', 'ଲୋକ']

docs.title: Custom stopword lists
docs.text:
Stopwords is a mutable collection you can start from the default, a file, or a corpus. add and remove return the same object, so calls chain.

>>> from openodia import Stopwords
>>> sw = Stopwords.default()
>>> "ଓ" in sw
True
>>> _ = sw.add("ରାମ").remove("ଓ")
>>> "ଓ" in sw, "ରାମ" in sw
(False, True)
>>> ud.remove_stopwords(text, stopwords=sw)
['ସୀତା', 'ଘରକୁ', 'ଯାଏ', 'ସେ', 'ଭଲ', 'ଲୋକ']
>>> small = Stopwords(["ରାମ"])
>>> ud.remove_stopwords(text, stopwords=small)
['ସୀତା', 'ଘରକୁ', 'ଯାଏ', '।', 'ସେ', 'ଭଲ', 'ଲୋକ', '।']

stopwords= also accepts a plain set, frozenset or list.

Stopwords.from_corpus(tokens, top_n=100) builds a list from the most frequent tokens of your own corpus, Stopwords.from_file(path) reads one word per line, and save(path) writes the list back. coverage(tokens) returns the fraction of tokens that are stopwords:

>>> round(sw.coverage(ud.word_tokenizer(text)), 3)
0.333

docs.title: Normalize and clean
docs.text:
The same visible string can have several encodings. normalize applies a Unicode normalization form (NFC by default). clean applies NFC, removes zero-width joiners and collapses whitespace.

>>> from openodia import normalize, clean
>>> normalize("ଡ" + "଼") == "ଡ଼"
True
>>> normalize("ଡ଼", form="NFD") == "ଡ" + "଼"
True
>>> clean("  ଓଡ଼ିଆ   ଭାଷା  ")
'ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଭାଷା'
>>> clean("ନମ" + "\u200c" + "ସ୍କାର") == "ନମସ୍କାର"
True

Digit conversion is off by default. Turn it on with CleanOptions:

>>> from openodia.text import CleanOptions
>>> clean("ଆଜି 123 ବର୍ଷ", options=CleanOptions(latin_to_odia_digits=True))
'ଆଜି ୧୨୩ ବର୍ଷ'
>>> clean("ଆଜି ୧୨୩ ବର୍ଷ", options=CleanOptions(odia_to_latin_digits=True))
'ଆଜି 123 ବର୍ଷ'
>>> clean(clean("  ଓଡ଼ିଆ  ")) == clean("  ଓଡ଼ିଆ  ")
True

Gotcha: the two digit options are mutually exclusive

Setting both latin_to_odia_digits and odia_to_latin_digits raises ValueError.

docs.title: Detect the language
docs.text:
ud.detect_language reports odia when more than threshold (default 0.5) of the non-space characters are in the Odia Unicode block, otherwise non-odia. The score is rounded to two decimals. Empty input returns {} and logs a warning.

>>> ud.detect_language(text)
{'language': 'odia', 'confidence_score': 0.91}
>>> ud.detect_language("hello world")
{'language': 'non-odia', 'confidence_score': 1.0}
>>> ud.detect_language("ରାମ hello", threshold=0.9)
{'language': 'non-odia', 'confidence_score': 0.62}

Gotcha: script, not language

This is a character-ratio check. Text in another language written in the Odia script scores odia, and Odia written in Latin letters scores non-odia.

docs.title: Translation and cache
docs.text:
Translate between Odia and other languages. English to Odia tries a bundled offline dictionary first and only then calls Google Translate. Results that come from Google are kept in a cache.

Examples that need the network have no output shown and are not run by the test suite, because Google can rate limit or change its answers. Everything else on this page is run by the suite.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Function Direction Default other_lang_to_odia(text, source_language_code="en") any language to Odia English source odia_to_other_lang(text, dest_language_code="en") Odia to any language English target universal_translation(text, source_language_code="en", dest_language_code="or") any to any English to Odia

Language codes are the ones Google Translate uses, for example hi, de, or.

from openodia import other_lang_to_odia, odia_to_other_lang, universal_translation

other_lang_to_odia("शेयर बाज़ार", source_language_code="hi")
odia_to_other_lang("ନମସ୍କାର", dest_language_code="de")
universal_translation("Guten Morgen", source_language_code="de", dest_language_code="en")

docs.title: The offline dictionary
docs.text:
When the source is "en", other_lang_to_odia looks the text up in an English to Odia dictionary that ships with the package. The lookup is case-insensitive and needs no network.

>>> from openodia import other_lang_to_odia
>>> other_lang_to_odia("good morning")
'ଶୁଭ ସକାଳ'
>>> other_lang_to_odia("Good Morning")
'ଶୁଭ ସକାଳ'
>>> from openodia.corpus.dictionary import get_dictionary
>>> dictionary = get_dictionary()
>>> len(dictionary) > 100_000
True
>>> dictionary["a bad apple"]
'ଏକ ଖରାପ ଆପଲ୍'

The dictionary is loaded once per process, so the first call pays for reading the JSON file and later calls reuse it.

Gotchas

  • The key is lowercased but not stripped. "good morning " with a trailing space misses the dictionary and goes to Google.
  • A non-English source never uses the dictionary, even for a word that is in it.
  • odia_to_other_lang and universal_translation always go to Google, never to the dictionary.

docs.title: The translation cache
docs.text:
Every Google answer is stored under the key (text, source_code, destination_code) in an in-memory LRU cache of 10,000 entries. cache.stats() reports hits, misses and sizes, and the same call repeated later is served from memory.

You can seed the cache yourself, which is also how to see a hit without the network:

>>> from openodia import cache, odia_to_other_lang
>>> cache.clear()
>>> cache.get_cache().set(("ନମସ୍କାର", "or", "en"), "Hello")
>>> odia_to_other_lang("ନମସ୍କାର")
'Hello'
>>> cache.stats()
{'hits': 1, 'misses': 0, 'size': 1, 'max_size': 10000, 'disk_size': 0}

cache.get_cache().get(key) returns None on a miss and counts it:

>>> cache.get_cache().get(("ଅଜଣା", "or", "en")) is None
True
>>> cache.stats()["misses"]
1

docs.title: Size and eviction
docs.text:
cache.configure(max_size=n) sets the capacity. The least recently used entry is evicted first, and reading an entry makes it the most recent.

>>> _ = cache.configure(max_size=2)
>>> c = cache.get_cache()
>>> c.set("a", "1"); c.set("b", "2"); c.set("c", "3")
>>> c.get("a") is None, c.get("c")
(True, '3')
>>> cache.stats()["size"]
2
>>> cache.configure(max_size=0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: max_size must be >= 1, got 0

Gotcha: configure starts a new cache

configure installs a fresh cache. Entries and hit counters from the old one are gone, and disk_path is dropped unless you pass it again.

docs.title: Persist across runs
docs.text:
Install the extra and give configure a directory:

pip install "openodia[cache]"

from openodia import cache

cache.configure(max_size=50_000, disk_path="~/.cache/openodia/translate")

Reads check memory first, then disk. You can also set the defaults before the process starts with the environment variables OPENODIA_CACHE_MAX_SIZE and OPENODIA_CACHE_DISK. An invalid size raises ValueError the first time the cache is used.
